messages.subject: Point count using animal vocals and estimating distance
parts:
Hello all,

I'm doing line transect distance sampling in North Madagascar in order=20
to estimates nocturnal lemurs densities.

But their are 2 species of lemurs that we never (or rarely) see on=20
transect but that we can hear really easily, because they sing mainly at=20
the moment we are doing night survey (Phaner and Eulemur).

And in all the forest it is obvious for us that they occur at high=20
densities.

In order to complete our study I'm planning to do Point count distance=20
sampling survey using animal vocals and estimating distance to observer.=20
But point count is new to me and none of the member of the team have=20
experience in it.

I'm wondering if this kind of survey would limit our analysis capacity=20
to encounter frequencies or relative densities....as we are violating=20
one of the assumption of the method : the distance from the observer=20

cannot be measured acurately.

If you have answers to my problem, suggestion to resolve it, ....

I think people doing bird survey can be confronted to the same problem=20
but quickly going true the litterature (available to me in madagascar=20
now) I have not been able to find answers to my question, clear and=20
simples protocols to do Point count distance sampling...
If you have good protocole, nice bibliograpics items, and nice answers,=20

you'd make my life aesier.
...


Thanks all of you


Jordi

messages.author: 6e15de0134e98c08
messages.subject: Re: Point count using animal vocals and estimating distance
parts:
Dear Jordi,

If your problem is using the acoustic data to apply conventional=20
distance sampling, that is in fact what happens for many bird surveys in=20
closed canopy habitats, and essentially people usually assume that=20
measurement error is small.

However, some published work implies that might not be the case, e.g.

Alldredge, M. W.; T. R. Simons & Pollock, K. H. A field evaluation of=20
distance measurement error in auditory avian point count surveys Journal=20
of Wildlife Management, 2007, 71, 2759-2766

On the other hand, if you need references on acoustic density surveys=20
you could use both

(using SECR for birds)

Dawson, D. K. & Efford, M. G. Bird population density estimated from=20
acoustic signals Journal of Applied Ecology, 2009, 46, 1201-1209

or

(using CDS for whales)

Marques, T. A.; Munger, L.; Thomas, L.; Wiggins, S. & Hildebrand, J. A.=20
Estimating North Pacific right whale (Eubalaena japonica) density using=20
passive acoustic cue counting Endangered Species Research, 2011, 13, 163-=
172

How you will see from this last reference, you have a potential problem=20
in relating the density of sounds to the density of animals, but this=20
can be solved in 2 ways: (1) using a cue rate (as we did in the above=20
reference) or assuming you can uniquely identify each bird to an animal=20
(as I believe Dawson and Efford have).

As an aside, I would be interested in knowing more details about your=20
study, as we are finalizing a review paper on estimating animal density=20
from acoustics data and yours seems like an interesting setting.

I hope this helps,

Cheers

Tiago

messages.author: 4a8db77441d75cfd
messages.subject: Re: Point count using animal vocals and estimating distance
parts:
Thanks a lot tiago for your answer

In fact you really well understod my problem.

Some more details about the study
We hear those 2 noctunal lemurs but have no way to see them. (It's not=20
the case for the 2 others nocturnal lemurs for which we are doing Line =20
Transect distance sampling.)
And yes my problem is that I have no way to be sure that we measure=20
distance to the animal accurately (as we do not see animals)
But we hear them repeatedly (from once to 30 times in 10 minutes) and=20
really well, we can hear animals at up to 200 meters (if we believe in=20
our distance estimates)
At each point, in 10 minutes we can hear up to 15-20 different=20
individuals (at least for one of the 2 species)
And its not very hard to differenciate individuals because they are=20
communicating, calling and answering to each other.
We have no recording material....................
And no range finder
and no way to see the heard animals
We are evolving in rough topography, dense tropical mountain forest in=20
north madagascar, so we cannot move from pointing count after the=20
counting period to identify the individuals.

We have only data for one forest yet... but I want to be sure I'm not=20
loosing my time doing this because I do not know a lot concerning point=20
count and analysis of point count when based on auditory survey.
I'm only used to visual distance sampling for which I'm now quite=20
confident in buiding survey and analysisng data. But Its a bit different

Well my last probelm is that I have no right acces for Journal of=20
Wildlife Management (so I could not red the alldredge paper)

Than I'm not sure about what you do call a "cue rate" ....

this is all

Thanks a lot for your last and future answers.

Jordi
